name: Echinocandins
route: IV infusion: daily (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) or weekly (rezafungin)
mechanism: Block glucan synthase, the enzyme fungi use to build their cell wall, so the wall weakens and the fungal cell bursts; human cells have no such enzyme
uses: Invasive aspergillosis when other drugs fail
Preventing Candida infection in stem cell transplant

article.summary: Echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin, rezafungin) are intravenous antifungal drugs and the usual first treatment for serious Candida bloodstream infections.
article.takeaway: Echinocandins are antifungal lipopeptides that block an enzyme fungi need to build their cell walls, a target human cells lack. Caspofungin, micafungin and anidulafungin are given by daily IV infusion, and the newer rezafungin once a week. US guidelines recommend an echinocandin as initial treatment for most people with a Candida bloodstream infection.[^1] In one head-to-head trial, anidulafungin worked in **75.6%** of patients versus **60.2%** with fluconazole.[^2] Most side effects are mild, with liver test changes and infusion reactions the main concerns.[^3]
glance: Candida bloodstream and deep-tissue infections and esophageal candidiasis; salvage use in aspergillosis
IV infusion over about an hour: daily, or weekly for rezafungin
Randomized trials against fluconazole and against each other, plus IDSA guideline support

blocks.text: Fungi, unlike human cells, are surrounded by a rigid wall. A key ingredient of that wall is a sugar polymer called 1,3-beta-D-glucan, which an enzyme called glucan synthase assembles. Echinocandins are large lipopeptides, meaning a ring of amino acids attached to a fatty tail, that jam this enzyme. Without a sound wall the fungal cell weakens and bursts.

Because people have no glucan synthase, the drugs are selective and usually well tolerated. They kill Candida yeasts but only slow the growth of Aspergillus molds, and they do not work against Cryptococcus or several other fungi. Their size means the gut cannot absorb them, so they have to be infused.
The four drugs share a core role in Candida infections but differ in their labeled uses.

rows: Candidemia and other Candida infections; esophageal candidiasis; presumed fungal infection in neutropenic fever; invasive aspergillosis when other therapy fails. Ages 3 months and up.[^3]
Candidemia and other Candida infections; esophageal candidiasis; preventing Candida infection in stem cell transplant. Ages 4 months and up.[^4]
Candidemia and other Candida infections (ages 1 month and up); esophageal candidiasis in adults.[^5]
Candidemia and invasive candidiasis in people 12 and older who have limited or no alternatives.[^6]

Day-14 global cure 59% vs 61%; day-30 deaths 24% vs 21%; noninferior on both[^8]

blocks.text: The 2016 Infectious Diseases Society of America guideline gives an echinocandin a strong recommendation as initial therapy for candidemia. Fluconazole is an acceptable alternative for selected patients who are not critically ill and are unlikely to have a resistant organism, and stable patients with susceptible Candida can switch to fluconazole after about 5 to 7 days.[^1]

All four are infused into a vein, generally over about an hour, and never as a rapid push. Caspofungin and anidulafungin start with a larger first-day dose, and micafungin has no loading dose. Rezafungin is given as 400 mg in week one and then 200 mg once weekly, and its label notes that safety beyond four weekly doses is not established.[^6] Bloodstream infections are usually treated until two weeks after blood cultures clear and symptoms resolve.[^1]

items: **Common reactions:** fever, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, low potassium and anemia. For rezafungin the label lists low potassium, fever and diarrhea most often.[^6]
**Liver:** liver enzyme rises occur, and each label includes a liver warning. Isolated cases of serious liver dysfunction have been reported, though a causal link is not established.[^5]
**Infusion and allergic reactions:** infusion-related reactions and, rarely, anaphylaxis are listed in the labels.[^6]
**Photosensitivity:** the rezafungin label warns of skin reactions to sun exposure.[^6]
**Interactions:** cyclosporine raises caspofungin levels and liver enzymes, tacrolimus levels can fall, and enzyme inducers such as rifampin call for a caspofungin dose change.[^3]

evidence.label: Strong: randomized trials and guideline support
evidence.text: Randomized trials show that echinocandins match or beat their comparators in candidemia and invasive candidiasis, and a major guideline recommends the class first.[^1][^2][^7] Evidence for aspergillosis is weaker, so the class is used there mainly after other drugs fail.[^3]

faq.q: Why are echinocandins given only by vein?
faq.a: They are large molecules that the gut barely absorbs. Once a patient is stable and the organism is susceptible, treatment is often switched to an oral antifungal such as fluconazole.[^1]

faq.q: How is rezafungin different from the older drugs?
faq.a: It is a newer echinocandin that stays in the body longer, so one weekly infusion replaces daily infusions. It was noninferior to caspofungin in ReSTORE, but it is labeled only for people with limited or no alternatives.[^8][^6]

faq.q: Do echinocandins treat every fungal infection?
faq.a: No. They are strongest against Candida. Activity against Aspergillus is limited, so caspofungin is labeled for invasive aspergillosis only when other treatments fail or are not tolerated, and the class does not treat Cryptococcus or several other fungi.[^3]

faq.q: How are they related to antibiotics like daptomycin?
faq.a: Both are lipopeptides, a ring of amino acids with a fatty tail. They hit different targets: echinocandins attack the fungal cell wall, while [daptomycin](/peptides/daptomycin) damages bacterial cell membranes.
